name: noria
summary: Noria's own cube, opening as an exact copy of Lorencia's so that adding it moves nothing until somebody looks at it.
why: Until this file existed the elf wood was graded through lorencia.json, and not by a
decision: index.py hangs a cube on the world whose name it shares, Lorencia was the only
cube in assets/grades, and the client fell through to `Grades.Values.First()`. So the one
town with a grade lent it to the other, silently, and the lending was invisible because
there was nothing to compare it against.
What was being lent is not neutral. lorencia.json is argued, at length, around one town's
palette: terracotta paving under a warm baked light, a shadow tint pushed hard toward blue
to break the single hue that palette kept collapsing into, and a highlight tint halved
again because the light was already warm four multiplies deep. Every one of those moves is
a correction to something Lorencia does and Noria does not.
Noria is the opposite problem on both axes. Its ground is 93.3% one olive turf, its baked
TerrainLight is neutral where Lorencia's is warm - (167, 167, 168) of 255 against
(141, 144, 144) - and through ground.py's curve that arrives 22% brighter with 18% less
spread in it. A grade built to warm the shade and cool the light of a terracotta town is
being asked to do neither of those things here, over a green frame that is already flatter
and brighter than the one the numbers were measured on.
NOTHING IS MOVED IN THIS FILE YET, AND THAT IS THE POINT OF IT. Every value below is
Lorencia's, to the digit, so the cube this bakes is the cube Noria was already being shown
through and adding it changes no pixel. What it changes is that the two towns can now
disagree, and that a change made for one stops arriving in the other.
The tuning is a pass on screen, not an arithmetic one. The measurement above says which
knob has the most to give back - the frame is bright and flat, so the contrast and the
shadow end are where the room is, and the shadow tint is the one number most likely to be
wrong in kind rather than in degree, since blue shade under a green canopy is a claim
about a sky the wood mostly hides. But a number chosen off a histogram and never looked at
is exactly what lorencia.json's own comment history is a record of getting wrong four
times in a row, and this file is not going to start by repeating it.
Note that the cube is currently switched off at the sheet - lighting.json has
"grade": false - so this bakes and is loaded and nothing reads it until that flips.
